SamMvuEL G. Draxeu, Esq.—The readers of the Register will learn with pleasure that 
our predecessor, Mr. Drake, is in good health and actively engaged in historical and 
antiquarian researches in England. Our last number contained three articles from his 
pen, which show that he is making good use of his time, and that he still bears the 
Register in mind. 


CENTENNIAL CELEBRATION OF THE CAPTURE OF QuEBEC.—This society has in- 
vited Hon. Lorenzo Sabine to deliver an address on the 13th of September, 1859, in 
commemoration of the capture of Quebec. The use of the hall of the Massachusetts 
House of Representatives has today (Sept. 7th) been secured, and before this number 
is issued, the celebration will, it is presumed, take place. We shall notice it more fully 
in January.

>THE Historical AND GENEALOGICAL REGISTER is issued Quarterly, in January, 
April, July, and October; each Number containing about ninety-six pages, octavo; making 
annually a volume of about four hundred pages. 


The price to Subscribers will be Two DoLLars a year, payable on issuing the first Number 
efeach Volume. Any person obtaining subscribers and becoming responsible for six copies 
of the work, shall be entitled to the seventh copy gratis. 


(> Twetve VoutvneEs of the Register being now completed, subscribers may exchange their 
numbers (if in good condition) for Bound Volumes, or have their own numbers bound—in full 
cloth, lettered and gilt, at 38 centsthe volume. A splendid die has been procured, representing in 
gold the Arms of al] the N. E. States, with which the backs are impressed. 


N. B.—Subscribers will observe,—that the Register is in no case sent to them after they have 
ordered it stopped, wnless such orderis not received till a new volume has commenced, and arrear- 
ages remain unpaid, according to the rules of periodicals. 


It is the wish of the Publisher to Register the name of every Subscriber to the work, that it 
may be known in after times who were the real promoters of The Recovery, Preservation, and 
Dissemination of the knowledge of the founders of this great American Union. He has, 
therefore, adopted the plan of crediting Subscribers to the Register with all moneys remit- 
ted in payment for the work, on the last page of each number. By this mode, every person 
will see, in the number succeeding his remittance, that he is duly credited for his current year’s 
subscription. 


{> Aathors and Publishers of Town or Locat HistoriEs, GENEALOGIES, &c. will find it 
to their interest to send a few copies to the office of the Publisher and Editor, for sale. 


{> Rooms oF tHE Society, No. 13, Bromfield Street. Regular monthly meetings of the 
Society, on the first Wednesday in every month, at 3 o’clock, P. M. 


THE PRINCE SOCIETY 


FOR 


MUTUAL PUBLICATION. 


” 





It has been a matter of regret for several years, that no feasible plan was pro- 
posed for the publication of valuable historical manuscripts, which exist in our 
various public libraries, and in the hands of individuals. It is evident that ne 
Historical Society has supplied the students of history with this class of books, 
except to a very moderate extent. It is believed that one volume a year is the 
best result yet attained by any society, and these publications have been of a very 
variable degree of value. In fact, from the organization of a Historical Society, 
it is evident that its main purpose must be, to collect those manuscripts, and en- 
courage that taste for investigation, in which this proposed Publication Society 
finds its materials and sees its prospect of success. 

On the 25th of May, 1858, a few gentlemen of this city organized a Society, 
whose object is the publication, on the mutual principle, of manuscripts relating 
to the early history of this country, and the reprinting of books on this subject 
which have become so scarce as to be found only in the great libraries in our 
principal cities. The plan of publication embraces not only the particular section 
of the United States in which the Society has originated, but includes the early 
history of all the Colonies; and it is hoped that patrons will be found in every 
State of our Union. 

From a feeling of veneration for the labors of the annalist of New England, 
the Rev. Tuomas Prince, this Society, inaugurated on the anniversary of his 
birth, has been named “ The Prince Society for Mutual Publication.” 

The plan of publication, and terms of membership, are so simple as to com- 
mend themselves to all. Any one who agrees to purchase of the Society its 
publications, becomes a member, and ceases to be such only when he declines to 
receive the books. Once a year (May 25th) the Society chooses its officers, 
seven in number, who constitute the Council for the ensuing year, and who su- 
perintend all publications during their term of office. No member is called on 
for a subscription, but when a volume is issued, the Council fixes its price, as 
near the actual cost as possible, and he pays for and receives his copy. A limit 
will be placed on the number and prices of volumes to be issued in any one year. 
For the first year, this limit will be three dollars. The fractional profits ensuing 
from the issue of each book will be reserved, and, when sufficient, will be used 
for the gratuitous publication of a volume for the members. 

The ordinary hindrance to the publication of historical works has been the 
want of a previous subscription. It has been found too laborious and expensive 
a task to issue proposals for every new work. But with a Society established, 
whose members are pledged to take its publications, it is possible to make perma- 
nent arrangements, and to secure many invaluable documents for its series. The 
members will be benefited by the comparatively low cost of their copies, and their 
value as of limited impression. The proposed form of the Society’s volumes is a 
small quarto. 

The present Council, having secured several valuable works to print, will neg- 
lect no opportunity to obtain others, and the assistance of all the members is 
requested to secure every document available for their series. 

Persons wishing to become members may address any of the officers named 
below, who, as before stated, constitute the Council of the Society. 


SAMUEL G. DRAKE, President. 


THOMAS WATERMAN, 
FREDERIC KIDDER, Vice Presidents. 
JEREMIAH COLBURN, 


JOHN WARD DEAN, Corresponding Secretary. 
JOHN WELLS PARKER, Treasurer. 
WM. H. WHITMORE, Recording Secretary. 
Boston, Dec. 2], 1858.

therefore, adopted the plan of crediting Subscribers to the Register with all moneys remit- 
ted in payment for the work, on the last page of each number. By this mode, every person 
will see, in the number succeeding his remittance, that he is duly credited for his current year’s

PROPOSALS, BY LITTLE, BROWN & CO., BOSTON, 


FOR PUBLISHING BY SUBSCRIPTION, , 
A Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New 
England, 
BY JAMES SAVAGE, 


FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE MASS. HISTORICAL SOCIETY. 


IN FOUR VOLUMES, OCTAVO. 





The work has been prepared on the basis of ‘ F'armer’s Register,” 
but on a plan much more extensive than the one adopted by that 
author, and, it is estimated, contains nearly six times the amount 
of matter. It will be published in four volumes, of about five 
hundred pages each, so that it may be interleaved and bound, 
without rendering the volumes inconveniently large ; or two vol- 
umes may be bound in one, as the subscriber shall prefer. 

It is proposed to issue two volumes in 1859, and the remaining 
two in 1860. 

The price will be $2.50 per volume, bound in cloth. 

N. B.—By a special arrangement with Messrs. Little, Brown & 
Co., the Publisher of the Register is authorized to furnish the 
above work on their terms to all those who may order it of him; 
and he hopes those who take and those who read the Register, 


will send him their names as Subscribers as early as possible. 
Boston, Aprit 1, 1859.

WILLIAM B. TRASK, WM. H. WHITMORE, JOHN WARD DEAN, 
Publishing Committee and Editors. 


The Publishing Committee, in their Address to the Readers of the Register in January last, 
announced their design of confining genealogical articles to the first four generations in this 
country, except occasionally bringing down a few lines to the present time. Some families, 
however, have expressed a wish to have later generations preserved in detail in the Register. 
The Committee are willing to do this by adding additional pages to the Register, if correspon- 


dents, or their friends, will pay the expense of the same. Our subscribers cannot complain of » 


a want of the usual variety, if this course is pursued. Eight pages are added in this way to 
the present number. 


H. G. Somersy, Esq., has returned to England, to continue his genealogical researches. 
His address is—“ Morley’s Hotel, Trafalgar Square, London, Eng”

[THe HistoricaL AND GENEALOGICAL REGISTER is issued Quarterly, in January, 
April, July, and October; each Number containing about ninety-six pages, octavo; making 
annually a volume of about four hundred pages. 


The price to Subscribers will be Two DoLtars a year, payable on issuing the first Number 
of each Volume. Any person obtaining subscribers and becoming responsible for six copies 
of the work, shall be entitled to the seventh copy gratis. 


(> TuirTEEN VoiumeEs of the Register being now completed, subscribers may exchange 
their numbers (if in good condition) for Bound Volumes, or have their own numbers bound— 
in full cloth, lettered and gilt, at 38 cents the volume. A splendid die has been procured, 
representing in gold the Arms of all the N. E. States, with which the backs are impressed. 


N. B.—Subscribers will observe,—that the Register is in no case sent to them after they have’ 


ordered it stopped, unless such order is not received till a new volume has commenced, and arrear- 
ages remain unpaid, according to the rules of periodicals. 


It is the wish of the Publisher to Register the name of every Subscriber to the work, that it 
may be known in after times who were the real promoters of The Recovery, Preservation, and 
Dissemination of the knowledge of the founders of this great American Union. He has, 
therefore, adopted the plan of crediting Subscribers to the Register with all moneys remit- 
ted in payment for the work, on the last page of each number. By this mode, every person 


will see, in the number succeeding his remittance, that he is duly credited for his current year’s 
subscription,

Society, on the first Wednesday in every month, at 3 o’clock, P. M. —

The late Henry Bond, M. D., of Philadelphia, having bequeathed to the New 
England Historic-Genealogical Society the balance of the sheets of his invalua- 
ble thesaurus of New England family history, 


The Genealogies and History of Watertown, 


that Society has placed this property in the hands of trustees, to be disposed of 
by them, and the proceeds invested in a fund, to be called, in honor of their
